title: Feelings & Health
description: How you feel, and what to say when you're not well: capek, lapar, kangen, pusing. There's no word for am: Saya capek is I'm tired.

items.registerNotes: Senang bertemu dengan Anda (nice to meet you). Also to like being somewhere: Saya senang di sini (I like it here).
Angry with someone: marah sama dia in speech, marah kepada dia in writing.
items.cultureNote: Showing anger in public loses face and rarely gets results. Stay calm and smile, even when complaining.

items.pitfallNote: No word for of: takut anjing (afraid of dogs). In speech, often takut sama anjing.

items.registerNotes: Capek is what everyone says; lelah is the written word. With friends, capek banget (so tired).

items.pitfallNote: There's no am: Saya lapar (I'm hungry). Often said laper.
Two syllables, ha-us, not like English house.

items.registerNotes: Saya sakit (I'm ill); Kaki saya sakit (my foot hurts). Sakit apa? asks what's wrong.
Friends and family ask Sehat? (Keeping well?), and Sehat-sehat, ya (stay well) is a warm goodbye.
Also fed up with something: Saya bosan makan mi (I'm sick of eating noodles). Often said bosen.
The everyday, warm word: Saya kangen keluarga (I miss my family). Rindu means the same in songs and writing.
Jangan khawatir (don't worry). The kh is a breathy h, and many people say kuatir.

items.pitfallNote: Pusing is dizziness or a light headache, and also feeling overwhelmed: Saya pusing is as often about work or money as about health.

items.registerNotes: No verb needed: Anak saya demam (my child has a fever). People also say badannya panas (he's running hot).

items.pitfallNote: You drink medicine, even tablets: minum obat (take medicine).

items.registerNotes: Address a doctor as Dokter or Dok. Ke dokter is to go to the doctor's.
